explanation: The program accepts an account without verifying that it signed the transaction. Attackers can invoke privileged instructions using arbitrary accounts.
The program trusts account data without validating that the supplied account belongs to the expected authority. Attackers may substitute accounts they do not own.
The program accepts a sysvar account without verifying its address. An attacker may provide a fake account that mimics the expected sysvar.
The program deserializes and trusts account data without verifying ownership. Malicious users can provide attacker-controlled accounts with forged data.
Different account types can share compatible memory layouts. Without discriminator validation, an attacker can make one account type impersonate another.
The program allows account initialization without enforcing proper initialization checks, enabling account takeover or state corruption.
The program performs cross-program invocations without validating the target program. Attackers may redirect execution to malicious programs.
The same mutable account may be supplied multiple times, causing unexpected state updates and logic manipulation.
Using non-canonical PDA bumps can allow attackers to generate alternative valid PDAs and bypass expected validation rules.
A PDA reused across multiple trust domains can allow one workflow to interfere with another, leading to privilege escalation or data corruption.
Improper account closure can leave reusable account state or permit account revival attacks after funds have been reclaimed.
